questions.prompt: How does Swift handle `switch` case fallthrough by default?

questions.prompt: How does a switch statement in Swift differ from a switch statement in C, and what patterns can a Swift case match? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Swift switch statements must be exhaustive
Explains that Swift switch cases do not fall through automatically
Mentions pattern matching such as ranges, tuples, or where checks

questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, a switch statement must be exhaustive, so every possible value must match a case or default. Unlike C, Swift cases do not fall through on their own, so you do not need break at the end of a case. Swift cases can also match ranges, tuples, multiple values, and extra where checks.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Control Flow

questions.prompt: What is the difference between while and repeat-while loops in Swift? When would you use each? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that while checks its condition at the start before running the body
Explains that repeat-while checks its condition at the end, so it runs at least once
Gives a clear example of when each loop fits

questions.modelAnswer: A while loop checks its condition before each pass, so the body never runs if the condition starts false. A repeat-while loop checks its condition at the end, so the body always runs at least once. Use while when zero passes should be allowed, and repeat-while when the code must run once before checking.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Control Flow

questions.prompt: Why does Swift require the else block of a guard statement to leave the scope? How does guard let differ from if let in variable scope? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that guard else must exit the scope so code after guard only runs when the check passes
Explains that guard let keeps unwrapped values available in the code block after the guard
Contrasts with if let, which keeps unwrapped values only inside its own braces

questions.modelAnswer: Swift requires the else block of a guard statement to leave the current scope. Using return, break, continue, throw, or fatalError guarantees the code after the guard never runs when the check fails. Unlike if let, which keeps unwrapped values inside its braces, guard let keeps them available in the rest of the code block. This keeps your main code flat and easy to read.

questions.prompt: Explain how pattern matching with where clauses works in Swift switch statements. Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that where clauses add an extra Bool condition to a switch case
Notes that the case matches only when both the pattern and the where check are true
Mentions that values bound in the pattern can be used inside the where check

questions.modelAnswer: A where clause adds an extra Bool check to a switch case. The case matches only when the pattern matches and the where condition is also true. You can use values bound by the pattern right inside the where check, such as testing if x == y in a tuple.

questions.prompt: What are labeled statements in Swift, how do they work with nested loops, and what extra variable do they help you avoid? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that a labeled statement gives a loop a name before it
Explains that break or continue with the label targets an outer loop
Notes that this avoids needing an extra Bool flag to stop an outer loop

questions.modelAnswer: A labeled statement puts a name and a colon in front of a loop, such as grid:. Inside nested loops, plain break or continue only affects the inner loop. Writing break grid or continue grid targets the outer loop directly. This lets you skip or exit the outer loop without adding an extra Bool flag.
